Fall Fine Motor Activities

Colleen Beck OTR/L
Colleen Beck, OTR/L is a pediatric occupational therapist and the owner and author of The OT Toolbox website. She manages all of The OT Toolbox social media accounts and runs the popular newsletter. Read about Colleen's experience and career as an occupational therapist, including how The OT Toolbox began on our About The OT Toolbox page: https://www.theottoolbox.com/about-us/ Colleen created The OT Toolbox in 2011 and since then has written thousands of blog posts designed to support therapy providers, educators, parents, counselors, admin, and caregivers in promoting the healthy development of kids. Check out Colleen's blog posts below:
  • by Colleen Beck OTR/L
  • September 9, 2026

Fall themes make it easy to work on fine motor skills using apples, leaves, pumpkins, acorns, farm themes, and other seasonal materials. But rather than choosing a fall activity simply because it fits the season, you can use the activities below to target specific fine motor needs.

Use this fall fine motor activity guide to find ideas for hand strength, finger dexterity, scissor skills, visual motor skills, and handwriting. Many of the activities can address several skills at the same time, so I’ve included ways to adapt them depending on what you are working on.

I want to work on (jump to the area that you are looking to support with Fall themed strategies):
  • Fall Hand Strength Activities
    • Apple Geoboard
    • Fall Play Dough
    • Apple Hole Punch
  • Fall Dexterity Activities
    • Fall Tree Geoboard
    • Apple Paper Clip Counting
    • Fall Pom Pom Transfer
  • Fall Scissor Skills
    • Apple Cutting Practice
    • Fall Cut-and-Paste Craft
  • Fall Visual Motor Activities
    • Fall directed drawing
    • Fall Pattern Blocks
    • Fall I Spy / Seek and Find
  • Fall Handwriting Activities
    • Fall Writing Prompts
  • No-Prep Fall Fine Motor Activities
  • Fall Fine Motor Activities
  • Planning Fall OT Sessions?

As the leaves begin to change colors and fall, and the pumpkin spice everything is in the air, it’s a great time of year to add some fall themed activities to your therapy toolbox or even just add to play! Try a few of these fall fine motor activities to encourage and strengthen fine motor skills, a tripod grasp, fall fine motor activities for preschoolers, fall ideas for toddlers, or fall occupational therapy activities!

Be sure to check out our free Fall Sensory Activities booklet. It’s full of family-friendly sensory activities that celebrate the season AND promote motor skills through sensory experiences. The activities in this free booklet are a fun way to encourage fine motor and gross motor movement and development through fall activities. Scroll to the bottom of this blog post to grab your copy!

Fall Hand Strength Activities

If you have questions about why hand strength is weak, be sure to check out our resource.

Apple Geoboard

We have an apple geoboard in The OT Toolbox Membership under our Apple themed activities. Have the child recreate the apple design by stretching rubber bands across the pegs of a geoboard. Pulling and positioning the bands provides resistance to the fingers and hands while also requiring precision and controlled release.

Works on: hand strength, finger strength, bilateral coordination, visual motor skills, motor planning.

Change the challenge: Use thicker or more resistant bands for additional resistance, or simplify the design when the visual motor demands are making the hand-strengthening portion too difficult.

Fall Play Dough

Play dough is always a fun activity no matter what time of year. It’s resistive and you can work on specific fine motor skills or positioning like a pincer grasp, tripod grasp, wrist stability, arch development, etc. Rolling, squeezing, pinching, and pressing provide different types of resistance for the small muscles of the hands. These play dough exercises are fun tools for finger strength exercises and grip strength exercises that don’t seem so much like “work”. 

The soft and squishy dough provides a tactile sensory challenge with proprioceptive sensory feedback.

Occupational Therapy Activity: We like to hide items in the play dough, like mini leaves, mini Fall erasers, Fall colored beads, etc. You can also use printable playdough cards like we have in The OT Toolbox Membership to create Fall themed shapes.

Other play dough ideas include:

  • Roll orange play dough into pumpkins and use the fingertips to pinch stems
  • Press seeds into the dough
  • Roll play dough snakes and cut with scissors and then and shape it around a pumpkin or a leaf. 

Apple Hole Punch

This is another resource we have inside The OT Toolbox Membership.

Occupational Therapy Activity: Draw or print an apple and have the child punch holes around its outside edge. Operating a hole punch requires sustained hand force while positioning the punch around the edge adds a visual motor component.

Fall Dexterity Activities

Dexterity involves using the fingers efficiently for small, precise movements. For the hands to move in a coordinated way in fine motor tasks, you need several areas. This is where sometimes the skills break down. Dexterity includes speed and precision, visual motor skills, and strength. These skills allow for manual dexterity, or coordinated precision, to happen. Those skills listed out are:

  • separation of the sides of the hand
  • open thumb web space
  • neat pincer grasp
  • arch strength and development
  • bilateral coordination
  • finger isolation
  • hand strength
  • finger strength
  • in hand manipulation, including translation, shift, and rotation

Fall manipulatives such as pom poms, seeds, mini erasers, paper clips, and small craft materials can turn simple seasonal activities into opportunities for finger manipulation.

Other examples for a Fall theme to work on dexterity, include:

Fall Tree Geoboard

This is another printable we have in The OT Toolbox Membership.

The cool thing is a printable like a geoboard activity can target different aspects of fine motor skills, like strength that we described above, as well as dexterity and coordination.

Occupational Therapy Activity: Manipulating rubber bands around individual pegs requires the child to use the fingertips to grasp, stretch, reposition, and release the bands with control. Encourage the child to use the fingertips rather than pulling primarily with the whole hand.

Apple Paper Clip Counting

These activities and paper clip activities are an easy way to address a variety of fine motor needs on the go. We have an apple paper clip activity in The OT Toolbox. It’s print and go. You can laminate it and use it over and over again with paper clips.

Occupational Therapy Activity: Have the child attach the correct number of paper clips to an apple counting card. Opening and positioning paper clips requires precise fingertip movements and can encourage bilateral hand use when one hand stabilizes the card.

Works on: fingertip precision, bilateral coordination, dexterity, eye-hand coordination and number concepts.

Fall Pom Pom Transfer

We love using craft pom poms in therapy. You can use them in many different ways to target each of the dexterity skills listed above. Here is our full list of fine motor activities with craft pom poms.

Occupational Therapy Activity: Use tongs or tweezers to move fall-colored pom poms into an ice cube tray, muffin tin, or small containers. Change the size of the pom poms or the type of tool to modify the precision required.

Fall Scissor Skills

We have many scissor skills resources on The OT Toolbox website and themed printables in The OT Toolbox membership.

Apple Cutting Practice

Use the Apple Cutting Practice pages (in The OT Toolbox membership) to work on cutting along lines and controlling the scissors as the child follows the visual path. Cutting requires the cutting hand and helper hand to perform different jobs at the same time: one hand opens and closes the scissors while the other stabilizes and rotates the paper.

Occupational Therapy assessment: Notice while the child cuts the shapes and paper strips, does the child:

  • hold the scissors with the thumb positioned upward?
  • use the helper hand?
  • rotate the paper?
  • stay near the line?
  • make smooth or choppy cuts?
  • reposition the scissors?
  • fatigue quickly?

Another idea:

Cut Leaves with Scissors. If you live in an area with colorful fall foliage, use those leaves to work on scissor skills! Kids will love to cut leaves into small pieces or snip shapes from leaves. Make art with the leaves by glueing them onto paper or just snip and cut! We worked on line awareness by adding lines to our leaves, but you could just work on snipping leaves in half or cutting around the edges. If you are in an area without colorful leaves that fall this time of year, just use paper leaves or whatever you’ve got in your area.

Fall Cut-and-Paste Craft

In The OT Toolbox membership, we have a farm-themed cut-and-paste craft, which is an ideal craft for executive function, direction following and scissor skills.

Occupational Therapy perspective: A cut-and-paste craft increases the demands beyond cutting alone. The child must cut the pieces, visually determine where they belong, orient them correctly, follow the assembly sequence, and glue them into position.

Works on: scissor skills, bilateral coordination, visual spatial skills, sequencing and direction following.

Fall Visual Motor Activities

Fine motor activities often have a visual motor component. A child may have adequate hand strength and dexterity but still struggle when a task requires them to copy a design, follow a line, locate a target, or coordinate what they see with how their hands move.

Fall directed drawing

Copying the fall themed designs like acorns, leaves, apples, and pumpkins requires the child to look at the model, move their pencil or crayon, determine where each line begins and ends, and reproduce the spatial relationships to make their own version of the shape.

We have several Fall directed drawing pages in The OT Toolbox membership.

Fall Pattern Blocks

Copying a pattern block design combines fine motor manipulation with visual discrimination and spatial awareness. The child must identify the correct piece, determine its orientation, and position it in relation to the other pieces.

Fall I Spy / Seek and Find

We have several Fall themed I spy activities. There are back to school items and Fall themed pages too.

Occupational therapy aspect: When a child does an I Spy page, they are practicing visual scanning, and figure-ground, and sustained visual attention. You can target one area by grading the others up or down using specific cues or physical prompts. I like using a cut out frame to make the viewing area smaller.

And then you can add a fine motor component. After finding each item, have the child circle it, cover it with a small manipulative, or use a clothespin to mark the corresponding picture.

Fall Handwriting Activities

I like using this printable set of Fall Writing Prompts (it’s inside The OT Toolbox membership for members as well).

Fall Writing Prompts

Fall writing prompts can be used to practice handwriting within a meaningful writing task rather than practicing isolated letters. Depending on the student’s needs, focus on one handwriting component at a time, such as line awareness, spacing, letter size, formation, or writing endurance.

In OT sessions, you can use the one set of cards to meet the needs of your whole caseload.

Emerging writer: Write one fall word.

Beginning writer: Write one sentence.

Developing writer: Respond to a short fall prompt.

Older student: Plan and write a paragraph.

No-Prep Fall Fine Motor Activities

You can also use items found out in the yard or in the home to target fine motor skills this time of year.

Leaves: tear, crumple, punch, cut, sort or string.

Acorns: pick up with tongs, sort, count or transfer.

Play dough: make pumpkins, apples, leaves and acorns.

Paper: cut leaves, tear paper for collages or make paper chains.

Clothespins: attach “leaves” to a cardboard tree.

Paper clips: attach to counting cards.

Fall Fine Motor Activities

These fall fine motor activities are ones that boost the skills kids need for tasks like pencil grasp, managing clothing buttons and other fasteners, manipulating small items, opening containers and so many other fine motor tasks! Enjoy the season of Fall with a fine motor twist!

Crunch leaves– This is a seriously satisfying activity, according to my kids! Read more about using the season’s finest splendour in a Fall Leaves occupational therapy activity that can be used to work on auditory processing, sensory play, bilateral coordination, crossing midline, and fine motor skills like arch development, grasp strength, separation of the sides of the hand, and more. 

Add fall fun to play dough with this Fall Fine Motor with Play Dough. It’s an easy way to encourage small hands to develop the strength needed in the intrinsic muscles of the hands as they manipulate play dough with a few extras from the season. Use a fall scented play dough to add to the activity.

Use Fall Leaves to work on Pre-Writing Lines and Visual Motor Skills. This is a fun way to work on visual motor skills needed for pre-writing tasks like forming and copying shapes and letters. Kids can work on crossing midline and the eye-hand coordination needed for writing, all using colorful fall leaves. This activity would work with acorns, seeds, or other small seasonal items too.

This Fall Leaves Craft uses leaf shapes to work on bilateral coordination, tripod grasp, eye-hand coordination, and more as kids create a seasonal fall craft. This fall craft may be better for older kids, but it’s a great introduction to sewing too.

There is just something about punching holes in leaves! Really boost that hand strength by Punching Holes in Leaves with a Hole Puncher. This activity uses fall leaves to strengthen the gross grasp of the hand while creating leaf confetti. Kids can pick up and manipulate the leaf holes to really work that pincer grasp. Glue the small circles onto a paper to along a line to promote more eye-hand coordination and fine motor skills.

This Pumpkin Stamp Art is an old craft our our website that really boosts fine motor skills with a fall pumpkin theme! Kids can create stamp art with a paper towel tube or toilet paper tube while working on skills like grasp and precision of grasp, crossing midline, and arch development. This is a great craft for a small group or for a therapy caseload to complete with various graded components based on individual needs.

Fall Fine Motor Apple Tree Activity– This is another fall fine motor activity that uses a hole puncher to really boost hand strength and gross grasp. Punching holes with a hole puncher allows kids to strengthen their hand strength while encouraging skills like bilateral coordination and eye-hand coordination. 

A Fall Fine Motor Apple Seed Activity can be just the thing for toddlers to practice eye-hand coordination needed to scoop and pour objects. This activity encourages pincer grasp, in-hand manipulation, separation of the sides of the hand and other fine motor skills like precision of grasp. What fun!

A fall fine motor craft like this Thumbprint Pumpkin Craft can be a powerful tool to promote separation of the sides of the hand, finger isolation, as well as strength and dexterity of the radial or precision side of the hand. This precision of the thumb that occurs in thumbprint fine motor crafts is especially important as distal thumb flexion can be helpful in dexterity in a tripod grasp when holding a pencil. 

Ahhh, sunflower seeds are a tool that can be used in so many fall fine motor activities for kids! From the pincer grasp needed to hold them to the in-hand manipulation necessary to manipulate them within the palm, sunflower seeds are a creative and fall festive way to encourage fine motor strengthening and development this season! Kids can make this Fall fine motor Sunflower Craft and really boost those fine motor skills with a fall craft that will look great hanging on the wall!

There’s another seed this season that plays a big part in the development and strengthening of fine motor skills! Pumpkin Seeds! Pumpkin seeds can be used to improve dexterity, grasp precision, in-hand manipulation, arch development, grasp strength, and so many other areas. Use food coloring or liquid watercolors to dye pumpkin seeds after they’ve been scooped out of a pumpkin. (Get the kids in on that fine motor task, too!)  The, use those colored pumpkin seeds to scoop, sort, drop, pinch, and play while building fine motor skills. You can find the directions to color pumpkin seeds and read all about why and how this activity helps kids build fine motor skills in our Fall Fine Motor Activity with Colorful Pumpkin Seeds activity.

THEN, use those colored pumpkin seeds to extend the fine motor fun even more by creating a Fine motor Fall Suncatcher that kids can make and hang on a window. Let the kiddos get in on hanging the suncatchers because working on a vertical plane is an awesome way to strengthen the core and proximal shoulder/shoulder girdle which is oh, so important for fine motor tasks!

One more way to address fine motor needs this fall is to save up those bread ties. The plastic bread ties that you find on loaves of bread or items like bagels are great for manipulating and strengthening fine motor skills. Kids will love this Bread Tie Ghosts Fall Fine Motor Activity where kids can manipulate and manage bread ties while strengthening fine motor skills this fall!

What are your favorite fall fine motor activities for kids?

Planning Fall OT Sessions?

You don’t have to create every activity yourself.

The OT Toolbox Membership includes ready-to-use fall resources for fine motor skills, hand strength, scissor skills, visual motor skills, handwriting, executive functioning, sensory processing, and more.

Choose the skill you’re working on, print the activity, and use it in your session.
